Q: Why this two items have different width in Jetpack Compose A:

The order of the modifiers is important.

You have to use:

TextField(
    //....
    modifier = Modifier
        .height(55.dp)
        .padding(start = value) //apply the padding before the width modifier
        .width(88.dp)
 )

Q: Query with LIKE / IN A:

Since the RDBMS is not specified in the question and tags, we can look at an example for Postgresql.

Using comma‑separated lists of values, as is already being actively discussed in this question (as well as in many other SO questions), is considered a wrong approach to database design.

In this case, the “article” table stores tickers in the form of a list.
It is proposed to create an additional table “article_ticker” (article_id, ticker_id) to normalize the database and use indexes for fast linking between these tables and apply filters.
Some DBMS extensions allow for more convenient and efficient work with such values. Of course, in a more formalized form — JSON or ARRAY. The structured nature of the list enables more efficient work with it.

I suggest considering an example using GIN (General inverted index).

GIN is designed for handling cases where the items to be indexed are composite values, and the queries to be handled by the index need to search for element values that appear within the composite items. For example, the items could be documents, and the queries could be searches for documents containing specific words.

Comma-delimited tickers list stored as array.

Table for example

CREATE TABLE article (
  article_id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY generated always as identity,
  title varchar(20),
  article_txt TEXT NOT NULL,
  tickers text array 
);

Sample data

INSERT INTO article (title,article_txt,tickers) VALUES 
 ('article1 title', 'article1 text', array['AAPL','IBM'])
,('article2 title', 'article2 text', array['F','IBM'])
,('article3 title', 'article3 text', array['DELL','TXN'])
,('article4 title', 'article4 text', array['ALP','META']);

Since the difference in approaches affects large tables, we’ll add more rows.

with src as ( -- full list of tickers
  select array['AAPL','IBM','F','IBM','DELL','TXN','ALP','META','TKT1'] AS ta
)
insert into article (title,article_txt,tickers)
select concat('article1 title',idx) AS title
    ,concat('article1 text',idx) AS article_txt
    ,array_sample(ta,cast(floor(random()*5)+1 as int))  AS tickers  -- arbitrary subset
from generate_series(1,429000) idx
cross join src;

Here we add rows with a list of tickers — an arbitrary subset of the full list.

The query that OP wants to implement looks like this in this case.

SELECT *
FROM article a
WHERE array['AAPL','IBM','DELL','UNP'] && tickers ;

I.e., select rows for which the condition array['AAPL','IBM','DELL','UNP'] && tickers at least one ticker from the row belongs to the list specified by the parameter.

Q: Should I use signal and slot before or after the http request via QNetworkAccessManager? A:

First, let me name things:

  • QNetworkAccessManager *manager emits the signal.
  • QObject* receiver is the object whose slot must be invoked.

Obviously, we all understand that, for the slot to be invoked, the call to QObject::connect must return before QNetworkAccessManager::finished is emitted.

In the Qt-provided snippet, the C++ standard guarantees QObject::connect returns before manager->get(...) does, and we also know manager->get(...) returns before QNetworkAccessManager::finished is emitted. All is good.

Your snippet is wrong because it is only almost certain to work but with important differences depending on what exactly is going on. First off, it relies on QNetworkAccessManager having an asynchronous API, as per its detailed description: you could not call QObject::connect in time if it was synchronous.

As manager's parent is receiver in Qt's snippet and in yours, both have the same thread affinity, so there are 2 scenarios.

If manager and receiver live in the current thread:

The code you wrote guarantees QObject::connect is called before the current thread returns control to its event loop.
AFAIK, QNetworkAccessManager is implemented so that finished is called during the event processing phase of the event loop, so you can be sure it will be OK.

With that said, I am unsure there is an explicit guarantee finished will be emitted no earlier than when events are processed in manager's thread.
If it works only because of an unspecified implementation detail, however stable the code is at this point, it is a theoretically weaker justification of your code's validity.

If manager and receiver do not live in the current thread:

Like above, finished is called during the event processing phase of the event loop (in manager's thread). Unlike above though, the only thing you can rely on to say that QObject::connect happens before finished is emitted is the fact that HTTP requests over the Internet are millions of times slower than your CPU.

With that speed difference, the slot "only" has a 99.99999...% chance of being called (the probability decrases if e.g. you send a HTTP request to a process on localhost though).

In the remaining ε%, QObject::connect will be called (in the current thread) after finished is already emitted (in the distinct thread where both object live), too late for the slot to be invoked.

If manager and receiver lived in different threads (impossible as per your code), things would then depend on the connection type, on top of the other limitations I described above.

In all cases, your code would:

  • at best be as valid as Qt's (but without relying on the same level of proof).
  • have chances to be less reliable.
  • be sensitive to changes made somewhere else in your code base.

Q: Item index in a for loop A:

You didn't show what result you really need but with real DataFrame you could merge both dataframes

result = pd.merge(train, Address_df_2, on="Address")

to can get all information in one dataframe:

  Address  Valued_Address
0       a               1
1       b               2
2       a               1
3       c               3

And later you may use directly result for other calculations or use column from result to replace values in train

train["Address"] = result["Valued_Address"]

Full working example

I used dataframes from @FredBill answer.

import pandas as pd

train = pd.DataFrame({"Address": ["a", "b", "a", "c"]})
Address_df_2 = pd.DataFrame({"Address": ["a", "b", "c"], "Valued_Address": [1, 2, 3]})

result = pd.merge(train, Address_df_2, on="Address")

print(result)

train["Address"] = result["Valued_Address"]

print(train)

Q: How to reduce the time taken to solve cses problem number 2? A: 
if i in numbers:

This is the problem. It actually loops through every number individually, making your code timeout.

To fix this, we can use the set data structure:

n=int(input())
numbers = list(map(int, input().split()))
innumbers = set(numbers)
for i in range(1,n+1):
    if i not in innumbers:
       print(i)

This code is faster because the set data structure is specially optimized for checking if a number exists or not. You can search up hashmaps to learn more about it.

Alternatively you can use the following code:

n=int(input())
numbers = list(map(int, input().split()));
print(n*(n+1)//2 - sum(numbers))

If no numbers are missing, the sum is n*(n+1)/2. When one number is missing, all we need to do is no_missing_sum minus missing_one_number_sum, to get the singular sum of that missing number. This is actually the most efficient solution, as it uses simpler operations and does not use the still somewhat costly set check operation.
